title: The snow letter
translation: One morning, after a beautiful snowfall, I had something to tell someone and sent a letter, without a word about the snow. The reply said: "You couldn't even write one line asking how I'm enjoying this snow? Why should I listen to anything from someone that tactless? I'm really very disappointed in you." I loved that.
She's dead now, so even a little thing like that stays with me.
original: {雪|ゆき}の{面白|おもしろ}う{降|ふ}りたりし{朝|あした}、{人|ひと}の{許|がり}いふべき{事|こと}ありて、{文|ふみ}をやるとて、{雪|ゆき}のことは{何|なに}ともいはざりし{返|かへ}り{事|ごと}に、「この{雪|ゆき}いかが{見|み}ると、{一筆|ひとふで}のたまはせぬ{程|ほど}の、ひがひがしからむ{人|ひと}の{仰|おほ}せらるる{事|こと}、{聞|き}き{入|い}るべきかは、かへすがへす{口惜|くちを}しき{御心|みこころ}なり。」といひたりしこそ、をかしかりしか。

literal: On a morning when snow had fallen delightfully, I had something to say to someone and sent a letter, and in the reply to it, in which I had said nothing about the snow: 'Should I listen to what is said by someone so perverse as not to write even one stroke asking how I see this snow? It is a very, very regrettable heart', (that person) had said: that was delightful.
Since (that person) is now someone who has died, even such a small thing is hard to forget.

notes.quote: 雪のことは何ともいはざりし
notes.text: The correspondent expected a word about the snow, even in a letter about something else. Forgetting it was a small failure of feeling, and she lets him know.
ひがひがし: 'warped, out of tune, tactless'. The scolding is half real and half play.
し, しか: the past auxiliary き, his own experience. The text does not say who the letter writer was; she is usually read as a woman, and the translation follows that.
The last sentence turns a funny memory into a memorial, without any change of tone.
